~~~{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

source("blog/_R/post_setup.R")

set_plot_accent_color("#00695C")

install_missing_packages(c(
  "dplyr",
  "ggplot2",

  "scales",

~~~

The Gini coefficient is often introduced with a Lorenz curve, or simply as a
number between 0 and 1. But what does it actually measure?

Let's start with ten people, their incomes, and no curve.

## Ten people, two groups

Group A has modest differences in income. Group B keeps the first eight
incomes unchanged, but the last two people now earn 40 and 60 instead of
15 and 20.

~~~{r}
#| label: create-income-example

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

incomes <- tibble::tibble(
  person = LETTERS[1:10],
  group_a = c(5, 5, 5, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 15, 20),
  group_b = c(5, 5, 5, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 40, 60)
)

incomes |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Person", "Group A", "Group B"),
    align = c("l", "r", "r")
  )
~~~

The total income is 100 in Group A (mean 10), and 165 in Group B
(mean 16.5). Higher total income does not necessarily mean a more equal
distribution.

## Compare every pair

With ten people, there are

$$
\binom{10}{2}=\frac{10\times9}{2}=45
$$

unique pairs. For each pair, take the **absolute difference** in income.
If both earn the same, that pair contributes zero. If their incomes are
far apart, it contributes more.

~~~{r}
#| label: calculate-income-pairs

income_long <- incomes |>
  pivot_longer(-person, names_to = "group", values_to = "income") |>
  mutate(group = recode(group, group_a = "Group A", group_b = "Group B"))

# Compare people within groups, excluding self-pairs and duplicates.
pairs <- income_long |>
  rename(person_i = person, income_i = income) |>
  inner_join(
    income_long |>
      rename(person_j = person, income_j = income),
    by = "group",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) |>
  filter(person_i < person_j) |>
  mutate(difference = abs(income_i - income_j))
~~~

Here are all 45 comparisons for each group. Each cell shows the income
difference; the empty half contains comparisons we would otherwise count twice.

~~~{r}
#| label: plot-income-pair-matrix
#| column: page

pairs |>
  mutate(
    person_i = factor(person_i, levels = rev(LETTERS[1:10])),
    person_j = factor(person_j, levels = LETTERS[1:10])
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(person_j, person_i)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = difference), colour = "#F8F9FA", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = difference, colour = difference >= 30),
    size = 2.8,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#E0F2F1", high = "#00695C") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#263238", "TRUE" = "#FFFFFF")) +
  facet_wrap(~group, nrow = 1) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "The same pairs, but larger gaps in Group B",
    x = "Second person",
    y = "First person",
    fill = "Absolute gap"
  ) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
~~~

Instead of adding the 45 cells by hand, we can group pairs by their
two income values. For example, in Group A there are three people
earning 5 and five earning 10, so there are $3\times5=15$ such pairs.
Each has a gap of 5, contributing $15\times5=75$ in total.

~~~{r}
#| label: summarise-income-pair-types

pair_types <- pairs |>
  mutate(
    lower_income = pmin(income_i, income_j),
    upper_income = pmax(income_i, income_j)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    comparisons = n(),
    difference = first(difference),
    contribution = sum(difference),
    .by = c(group, lower_income, upper_income)
  ) |>
  filter(difference > 0) |>
  arrange(group, lower_income, upper_income)

pair_types |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Group", "Lower", "Higher", "Pairs", "Gap", "Contribution"),
    align = c("l", rep("r", 5))
  )
~~~

Pairs with equal incomes contribute zero. Adding the remaining contributions
gives **230 for Group A** and **765 for Group B**.

## Why normalize by population size and total income?

For nonnegative incomes $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, Gini is

$$
\boxed{
G = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i<j}|y_i-y_j|}
{\displaystyle n\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_i}
}
$$

The numerator is the sum of absolute differences over all unique pairs.
The denominator makes those gaps comparable:

- **Population size ($n$)** accounts for how the number of pairwise
  comparisons grows with the number of people.
- **Total income ($\sum y_i$)** makes the gaps relative to the income
  available in that population.

In our example:

$$
\begin{aligned}
G_A &= \frac{230}{10\times100} = \boxed{0.230},\\[6pt]
G_B &= \frac{765}{10\times165} \approx \boxed{0.464}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that Group B's total income also increased. Yet its differences
increased enough that Gini almost doubled.

Another equivalent interpretation is

$$
G = \frac{\text{average absolute difference between two incomes}}
{2\times\text{average income}}.
$$

Here we average over **all ordered pairs**, including the possibility
of selecting the same person twice. This also explains why multiplying
every income by 10 leaves Gini unchanged.

Let's verify the result directly in R.

~~~{r}
#| label: calculate-gini-by-group

income_summary <- income_long |>
  summarise(
    people = n(),
    total_income = sum(income),
    mean_income = mean(income),
    .by = group
  )

gini_summary <- pairs |>
  summarise(
    pair_count = n(),
    difference_sum = sum(difference),
    .by = group
  ) |>
  left_join(income_summary, by = "group") |>
  mutate(gini = difference_sum / (people * total_income)) |>
  arrange(group)

gini_summary |>
  select(group, pair_count, difference_sum, people, total_income, gini) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Group", "Pairs", "Sum of gaps", "People", "Total income", "Gini"),
    digits = 3,
    align = c("l", rep("r", 5))
  )
~~~

## Where does the Lorenz curve come from?

Only now do we need a curve. Sort the people by income, then accumulate
their share of the population and their share of total income.

~~~{r}
#| label: calculate-lorenz-curves

lorenz <- income_long |>
  group_by(group) |>
  arrange(income, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    population_share = row_number() / n(),
    income_share = cumsum(income) / sum(income)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(group, population_share, income_share) |>
  bind_rows(tibble::tibble(
    group = c("Group A", "Group B"),
    population_share = 0,
    income_share = 0
  )) |>
  arrange(group, population_share)
~~~

~~~{r}
#| label: plot-lorenz-curves

ggplot(lorenz, aes(population_share, income_share, colour = group)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#9E9E9E", linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Group A" = "#00897B",
    "Group B" = "#D84315"
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Two distributions, two Lorenz curves",
    subtitle = "The diagonal represents perfect equality",
    x = "Cumulative share of people (poorest to richest)",
    y = "Cumulative share of income",
    colour = NULL
  )
~~~

Group B bows farther below the equality diagonal. The usual area formula,

$$
G = 1 - 2\times\text{area under the Lorenz curve},
$$

gives exactly the same numbers as the pairwise calculation.

~~~{r}
#| label: verify-lorenz-area

lorenz_summary <- lorenz |>
  summarise(
    area = sum(
      diff(population_share) *
        (head(income_share, -1) + tail(income_share, -1)) / 2
    ),
    .by = group
  ) |>
  mutate(gini_from_lorenz = 1 - 2 * area) |>
  arrange(group)

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  gini_summary$gini,
  lorenz_summary$gini_from_lorenz
)))

lorenz_summary |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, align = c("l", "r", "r"))
~~~

## Takeaway

The Gini coefficient does not start with a curve. It starts with
**differences in income between pairs of people**:

- Add the differences across the 45 unique pairs.
- Normalize by population size and total income.
- Get 0.230 for Group A and 0.464 for Group B.
- See the same inequality as an area on the Lorenz curve.

Changing only two incomes nearly doubles Gini. The pairwise view
shows exactly why.

*Small-sample detail:* With ten people, the maximum Gini under this
definition is 0.9 (when one person receives all income). The maximum
approaches 1 as the population grows.
